## Solution

**Lower bound.** The sequence $\{a_n\}$ is strictly increasing and consists of natural numbers (positive integers), so $a_n \ge n$ for every $n$. In particular $a_{10} \ge 10$.

**Construction achieving $a_{10}=10$.** Set $a_n = n$ for $n=1,2,\dots,10$. We extend the sequence for $n\ge 11$ as follows.

Let $p_0,p_1,p_2,\dots$ be an infinite list of distinct primes. For each $n\ge 11$, consider the system of congruences
$$x \equiv -j \pmod{p_j}, \qquad j=0,1,\dots,n-11.$$
Since the moduli $p_0,\dots,p_{n-11}$ are pairwise coprime, the Chinese Remainder Theorem gives a unique solution class modulo $M_n=\prod_{j=0}^{n-11}p_j$. Define $a_n$ to be the smallest positive integer in this residue class that exceeds $a_{n-1}$. Such an integer exists (the residue class is infinite), and the choice guarantees $a_n>a_{n-1}$, so the sequence stays strictly increasing.

**Verification of the condition.** Fix any $k\ge 0$. For every $n\ge 11+k$, the defining congruences include $a_n\equiv -k\pmod{p_k}$, hence
$$p_k \mid (k+a_n).$$
Since $a_n\to\infty$, for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $k+a_n>p_k>1$, so $k+a_n$ is composite. Therefore the only indices $n$ for which $k+a_n$ can be prime satisfy $n\le 10+k$, a finite set. Thus $\{k+a_n\}$ contains only finitely many primes.

This holds for every $k\ge 0$, so the sequence satisfies the required property, and it has $a_{10}=10$.

**Conclusion.** Combining the lower bound $a_{10}\ge 10$ with the construction giving $a_{10}=10$, the smallest possible value is

$$\boxed{10}.$$
